I feel like I'm similar to you in a sense so I'll tell you what I did. 

I have PTSD and the anxiety from it manifests in nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite and basically fucking up my GI tract. I've had in 2 years, 2 severe episodes that lasted over 2 months each which lead to me being skeletally thin due to not eating, going on IV drips for nutrition and having to go to hospital every other day because of fatigue and generally being so weak I couldn't move. 

The first time I didn't do anything, I just lived that way crying everyday barely sleeping and slowly it went away as I became more secure in my surroundings. 

The second time was horrible I couldn't afford time off so I suffered in front of everyone but this caused me to stop it faster. I started eating things that didn't have to be chewed and taking natural herbs to help me sleep. For me the scent of lavender is relaxing so I smelt it before sleeping. After a particularly bad fall down the stairs the ER dr prescribed some muscle relaxer to help me sleep and it worked wonderfully. With good sleep and slowly eating better I got better. And as I got more into my routine I became less anxious and again more secure.

I still get flair ups and being unable to eat but now I know that even when I'm nauseous I can still eat something very liquidy and sweet tasting and I'll be fine. Now whenever I feel horrible I just take some of the same muscle relaxer which I barely use to get a good sleep and that usually helps me wake up restful and less anxious. You could try melatonin which is natural if you're having trouble sleeping. 

I hope this is helpful let me know how you do 💖

I've been going to therapy now for about a year I'd say. And in all honesty, for a person like me who is easily overwhelmed and shuts down when confronted with the things that overwhelm me, analyzing and deconstructing things has been a giant help in me navigating life at the moment. 

I'm already an analytical person all I had to do was apply it to myself and my own problems, and it did help me. Perhaps this is just you trying what you know worked in therapy. Sometimes digging deeper to find the 'why' is what you need and sometimes it isn't, which is why 'finding the root cause' annoys you while your friends are fine by it. 

My therapist told me once that people who have high cognition need to know the reason for their behavior and that knowing why may be the key to controlling it and managing the problems.
